$comment: The highest-leverage text in the repo. Meshy's reconstruction quality is mostly a function of how clean the reference image is. The asset-list skill fills ONLY the {{description}} and {{materialNotes}} slots -- it must never hand-write this boilerplate, or 150 assets drift apart visually.

thai-street-photoreal-v1.label: Thai street, photoreal prop plate
thai-street-photoreal-v1.textureSuffix: Physically based materials. Surface detail must come from fine relief -- pitting, grain, weave, weld beads, scratches -- not from painted-on shading. No baked lighting, no baked ambient occlusion, no painted shadows in the base colour.
$notes: One image, not a four-view sheet. The turnaround bought a little reconstruction accuracy and cost a splitter, a rejection loop and a 50x more expensive image model; a single three-quarter plate is what Meshy's image-to-3d wants anyway.
50% grey backdrop, not white: white or bright props vanish into a white matte and Meshy's background separation eats them.
'no cast shadow / no ground plane' is repeated deliberately -- it is the most-ignored instruction, and baked contact shadows become permanent dark smears on the albedo.

The camera clause comes FIRST and shouts. A cheap fast model reads the opening line hardest: with the same clause buried after the object description, flux/schnell returned a flat straight-on elevation, which reconstructs as a slab. Moved to the top and made blunt, the same seed budget returns the top face. The three-quarter angle is what carries the depth cues when there is only one image.

The 'Form' paragraph is the cheapest poly-count control there is. A bottle crate drawn as a dense lattice of slots reconstructs as topology the simplifier cannot cut -- it stalled at 6002 triangles against a 2500 target even at a 0.05 error ceiling. Simplifying the object at the image stage costs a third of a cent; fighting it downstream costs a whole regeneration loop.

The Form paragraph must never contain the words 'low-poly' or 'low-polygon'. The prompt ends with 'not low-poly' for a reason -- a faceted render reconstructs badly and violates the kit's notLowPoly rubric axis. Constrain the object's SHAPE without handing the image model a style cue it will happily obey.

Contact shadows survive a whole paragraph of negations. Image models follow a positive description far more reliably than a list of prohibitions, so the backdrop clause STATES that the object floats with nothing beneath it, and keeps the negations as backup.

The 50% grey backdrop is asked for and often ignored -- a cheap model hands back a white product matte instead. That is fine and no longer worth fighting: prepare-image.mjs MEASURES the backdrop and pads with it, so the plate is consistent whatever colour arrives.
thai-street-photoreal-v1.image:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: {{description}} {{materialNotes}}

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

thai-signage-photoreal-v1.label: Thai street, photoreal sign plate
thai-signage-photoreal-v1.textureSuffix: Physically based materials. Surface detail must come from fine relief -- pitting, grain, weave, weld beads, scratches -- not from painted-on shading. No baked lighting, no baked ambient occlusion, no painted shadows in the base colour.
$notes: A near-clone of thai-street-photoreal-v1 for ROAD SIGNS ONLY, and the only profile in the kit that permits text.

The base profile ends its negatives with 'no text, no labels, no arrows'. For every other prop that is correct -- baked lettering becomes a permanent wrong label on the albedo. For a sign it is fatal: the legend IS the object, and a blank blue plate is not a soi sign. This profile drops 'no text', 'no labels' and 'no arrows' and adds a positive Legend paragraph in their place.

The Legend paragraph is POSITIVE and specific, following the same lesson the base profile's backdrop clause records: image models obey a positive description far more reliably than a prohibition, and 'no text' was previously winning against any amount of lettering asked for in the description slot.

'no borders' was dropped from the negatives and rewritten as 'no border around the photograph itself'. The original wording was about the image frame, but almost every Thai road sign has a painted border inset from its edge, and the bare word was talking the border off the sign face.

The camera clause is left at the base profile's HIGH THREE-QUARTER 30 degrees on purpose. A flatter angle would render the legend more cleanly but reconstructs as a slab, which is the exact failure the base profile's notes were written to prevent; the Legend paragraph instead demands the face stay legible despite the angle.

Expect Thai glyphs to come back imperfect from a cheap fast model. That is acceptable here -- the plate is a reconstruction and framing reference, and the final legend is the texture stage's job. What this profile buys is a face that carries lettering at all, in the right places and the right colours.

thai-skyline-imposter-v1.label: Bangkok skyline, billboard imposter elevation

generation.aspect_ratio: PER ASSET: the narrowest supported ratio that is still wider than the asset's declared w:h, from 1:8, 1:4, 9:16, 2:3, 3:4, 4:5, 1:1, 5:4, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, 4:1. Each imposter asset records its ratio in notes.
generation.keepRaw: The RAW output is the imposter texture and must be kept beside the asset (assets/<id>/imposter.png or .webp). assets/<id>/preview.jpg from prepare-image.mjs is a 1024-square registry plate only and is NOT the texture source.

$notes: For SKYLINE IMPOSTERS only: a single upright quad carrying the plate as its texture, placed 150-300 m out beyond the playable area and yawed to face the camera. Nothing is reconstructed from this plate -- no Meshy, no sculpt -- so every choice the prop profiles make for reconstruction is reversed here.

STRAIGHT-ON elevation, not the prop profiles' high three-quarter: a billboard has one face and any foreshortening or keystone is baked in forever. Telephoto from far away keeps the verticals parallel.

Portrait and high resolution through the generation block, because a 300 m x 45 m tower on a 1024 square plate is ~115 px wide. flux/schnell and square_hd are wrong here; thaikit-preview-image must honour this block when the profile is this one.

The backdrop stays flat #808080 like the rest of the kit so prepare-image.mjs measures and validates it unchanged, and so the key to alpha is one flat fill. No sky and no ground is the hard part: a cheap model draws a skyline scene by reflex, so the backdrop clause states positively that grey fills where the sky and ground would be.
The Form paragraph is gone. Detail is free on a quad; every floor, mullion and balcony should resolve, because the texture is the whole asset.
Text is permitted only where the description asks for it (an LED wrap, a rooftop letter sign) and must be generic -- no real brand marks.
thai-skyline-imposter-v1.image:
Straight-on ELEVATION photograph of one whole high-rise building, taken from very far away with a long telephoto lens: the camera is level with the building's mid-height, so every vertical edge is perfectly vertical and parallel with no keystone convergence, and the main facade is seen frontally with only a thin sliver of one side. Not a three-quarter view, not an aerial view, not looking up from the street.

The building: {{description}} {{materialNotes}}

Whole building: the complete tower from its ground-floor base to the very top of its crown, roof plant, spire or antenna, with nothing cropped. The base sits at the bottom of the silhouette with nothing in front of it: no trees, no street, no cars, no people, no neighbouring buildings, no scaffolding. The only text is lettering explicitly described above; otherwise no signs, no logos, no watermarks, no annotations.

Framing: the building is centred and fills about 85% of the frame along its longer axis, with a clear empty margin on every side.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080) fills every part of the frame that is not the building, including where the sky would be and where the ground would be. The building is a cut-out floating against an infinite flat backdrop. No sky, no clouds, no horizon, no ground plane, no cast shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient, no haze, no atmospheric fade.

Lighting: bright overcast daylight, flat and even, soft and shadowless, so the facade reads as true albedo with its glass tint, concrete and paint colours exactly as described. No sun glare, no specular blowout, no lens flare, no dramatic sky colour reflected in the glass.

One building only. Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, every floor, window, mullion and balcony resolved, realistic weathering and grime. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render, not a wireframe, not low-poly.

thai-ground-tile-seamless-v1.label: Thai ground, seamless tiling surface plate
thai-ground-tile-seamless-v1.textureSuffix: Physically based material. Surface detail must come from fine relief -- aggregate, grain, joints, chamfers, ruts, tufts -- not from painted-on shading. No baked lighting, no baked ambient occlusion, no painted shadows in the base colour.
$notes: The ONLY profile in the kit whose plate is not a photograph of an object. A flat-quad ground tile is two triangles: the prop IS its texture, so the plate has to be the texture rather than a picture of a slab of it. That inverts every rule the prop profile is built on -- there is no camera angle, no silhouette, no backdrop, no margin, and the object must fill 100% of the frame, which the prop profile rejects at 75%.

It is generated by fal-ai/patina/material, not by flux/schnell, because SEAMLESS is the contract and no general text-to-image model can honour it. patina returns genuinely tiling output plus the basecolor/normal/roughness/height/metalness set the tile then binds. It is the same generator scripts/tilekit/substrates.mjs already uses for the road substrates.

Run it with enable_prompt_expansion FALSE. The expansion is an LLM rewriting the prompt for richer detail, which is exactly what this scaffold exists to prevent: it reintroduces the camera, the scene and the props that every clause below spends its words removing.
tiling_mode must be "both". "horizontal" or "vertical" wraps one axis and leaves the other seamed, and a ground tile is dropped on a grid in both directions.

The scale clause is stated in METRES and it is the highest-leverage line here. A material model has no idea how big the surface is, and the same prompt at the wrong scale gives cobbles the size of cars. Every tile in this set covers 8 x 8 m, so the plate must show that much ground and no more.

The negations are aimed at what a material model actually gets wrong: it draws a kerb along the bottom, a wall at the top, or a single hero object in the middle, because its training data is photographs of ground rather than ground textures. Stating the frame is an infinite continuation is what stops it.

prepare-image.mjs --flat is the matching gate. It skips every object test (all of which reject a correct texture) and measures the WRAP instead, against the image's own adjacent-line floor rather than a constant -- cobble and smooth concrete differ tenfold in ordinary adjacent-pixel detail, so a fixed threshold means nothing.
thai-ground-tile-seamless-v1.image:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: {{description}} {{materialNotes}}

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.
